According to Figure 3 in the technical report, the task categories include debugging, new feature, refactor, understanding codebase, documentation, testing, code review, optimize, devops, migration, deletion, and other categories. Notably, in later stages of training, simple heuristics such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: Which of the following is a task category used in Composer 2's RL training distribution?
questions.explanation: According to Figure 3 in the technical report, the task categories for RL training include debugging, new feature, refactor, understanding codebase, documentation, testing, code review, optimize, devops, migration, deletion, and other. Debugging is explicitly listed as a primary task category. The other options (weather forecasting, image classification, sentiment analysis) are not software engineering tasks and are not mentioned in the training distribution.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 demonstrates strong performance on CursorBench, the internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions. On CursorBench-3, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% accuracy, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 which scored 44.2%, and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 which scored 38.0%. These evaluations run agents directly within Anyrun infrastructure, the same infrastructure that supports the reinforcement learning pipeline. For each task, the codebase environment is initialized with the initial task prompt, and the agent executes exactly as it would in production.
questions.question: What percentage accuracy does Composer 2 achieve on CursorBench-3?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench tasks differ structurally from public evaluation sets in two key ways. First, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Second, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering, where developers must synthesize context from production logs, sparse bug reports, and large existing codebases.
questions.question: True or False: CursorBench tasks require more lines of code changes and have shorter problem descriptions compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench.

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale training, high availability, and independent scaling. These services include training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The training service uses a fully asynchronous stack built on Ray and PyTorch with a centralized reconciler for sample lifecycle state management. The environments service runs on Anyrun, an internal compute platform for running untrusted code at scale, with each pod being a dedicated Firecracker VM. Inference is partnered with Fireworks AI, and evaluations use a pinned version of the production backend and Cursor client.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four decoupled services in the RL infrastructure?
questions.explanation: The four decoupled services are training, environments, inference, and evaluations. This design enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding.

questions.lessonContent: In the CursorBench evaluation process, we first initialize the codebase environment and set up the initial task prompt for each benchmark task. Then, we run the Cursor agent on this task using the same infrastructure that supports our reinforcement learning pipeline. Finally, we execute the agent exactly as it would operate in our production environment to ensure faithful evaluation of real-world performance.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation workflow?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. There is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, though they recommend keeping them concise and human-readable. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations including the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of the directory where you run claude, and your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md).
questions.question: What is the name of the special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in multiple locations to control when they are pulled into context. You can place them in the root of your repo (the most common usage), where you should name it CLAUDE.md and check it into git so that you can share it across sessions and with your team. Alternatively, you can name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md files in any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos, or in any child of the directory where you run claude, where Claude will pull them in on demand when you work with files in those child directories.
questions.question: True or false: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) to apply to all your Claude sessions.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (with the former recommended for team sharing), or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following IS a way to manage Claude's list of allowed tools?
choices: Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session
Use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code
questions.explanation: The four valid ways to manage allowed tools are: "Always allow" prompts, the /permissions command, editing config files (.claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json), and the --allowedTools CLI flag. The --dangerously-skip-permissions flag is used to bypass all permission checks entirely, not to manage the allowed tools list.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Core Workflows and Optimization Techniques
questions.lessonTitle: Thinking Budget Levels in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, using specific trigger phrases allocates progressively more thinking budget. The phrase "think" triggers extended thinking mode with additional computation time to evaluate alternatives. These specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget: "think" provides the smallest boost, followed by "think hard", then "think harder", and finally "ultrathink" which allocates the maximum thinking budget. Each level allows Claude to more thoroughly analyze complex problems before providing a solution.
questions.question: What is the correct sequence of thinking budget trigger phrases, from smallest to largest?
questions.answer: think < think hard < think harder < ultrathink

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Core Workflows and Optimization Techniques
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can effectively handle many git operations including searching git history. Engineers commonly use Claude to answer questions like "What changes made it into v1.2.3?", "Who owns this particular feature?", or "Why was this API designed this way?" However, it helps to explicitly prompt Claude to look through git history to answer these queries. Simply asking about historical changes without explicit direction to check git history may not yield the desired results.
questions.question: True or false: Claude will automatically search through git history when you ask questions about past changes without explicitly asking it to check the git history.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Core Workflows and Optimization Techniques
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports several common workflows, but one is particularly effective for changes that are easily verifiable with tests. This workflow involves asking Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs first, then telling it to run the tests and confirm they fail before writing any implementation code. After committing the tests, you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests while instructing it not to modify the tests. Claude will iterate through writing code, running tests, and adjusting until all tests pass. This approach gives Claude a clear target to iterate against.
questions.question: Which workflow pattern involves asking Claude to write tests first, confirm they fail, and then write implementation code that makes those tests pass?
choices: Write tests, commit; code, iterate, commit
questions.explanation: The 'write tests, commit; code, iterate, commit' workflow is the test-driven development pattern where Claude writes tests first, you commit them, then Claude writes code to make those tests pass through iteration

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Core Workflows and Optimization Techniques
questions.lessonTitle: Explore, Plan, Code, Commit Workflow Ordering
questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for solving many problems. First, ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs to understand the codebase. Then, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem - this step benefits from using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode. Finally, ask Claude to implement its solution in code. This sequence ensures Claude researches and plans before jumping to code, which significantly improves performance for problems requiring deeper thinking.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow?
choices: Ask Claude to read relevant files

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: Safe YOLO Mode and Permission Bypassing
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes a headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Instead of supervising Claude, you can use the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag to bypass all permission checks and let Claude work uninterrupted until completion. This works well for workflows like fixing lint errors or generating boilerplate code. However, letting Claude run arbitrary commands is risky and can result in data loss, system corruption, or even data exfiltration through prompt injection attacks. To minimize these risks, the documentation recommends using --dangerously-skip-permissions in a container without internet access, such as following a reference implementation using Docker Dev Containers.
questions.question: What is the CLI flag to bypass all permission checks in Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: Claude Code as MCP Server and Client
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can leverage more complex tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol) and REST APIs. Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, allowing it to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config when running Claude Code in a directory, in global config for all projects, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file to make tools available to anyone working in the codebase. When working with MCP, it can be helpful to launch Claude with the --mcp-debug flag to help identify configuration issues.
questions.question: True or false: Claude Code can function as both an MCP server and client.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Automation and Multi-Agent Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees offer a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts when running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously. This approach allows you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For example, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component. To create a worktree, you use the command git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a, then launch Claude in each worktree with cd ../project-feature-a && claude.
questions.question: Which approach allows you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories?
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Image Pixel Structure and Color Representation
questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous but are actually composed of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (no color) to 255 (maximum intensity). For example, an orange color might be represented as rgb(255, 147, 41). An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel needs 3 bytes for RGB, the uncompressed file size is approximately 6.2 megabytes. Images can also include a fourth channel called alpha for transparency, which changes RGBA to use 4 bytes per pixel instead of 3.
questions.question: What is the numerical range for each color channel (red, green, blue) in a pixel?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression works by throwing away parts of the data that humans won't notice. JPEG exploits how human vision works: our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. We notice blurry edges but won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG first converts pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution since our eyes won't notice. It divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components, throwing away high-frequency details that represent fine edges. This allows files to become 10-20x smaller with minimal visible difference, but you cannot recover the original pixels.
questions.question: In lossy compression like JPEG, high-frequency components representing fine details like sharp edges are thrown away while smooth gradients are kept.

questions.lessonContent: PNG files organize their compressed data into structured chunks, each serving a specific purpose within the file format. A PNG file begins with a signature to identify it as a valid PNG file, followed by required chunks including IHDR (the image header containing metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual compressed image data), and IEND (the end marker). The IHDR chunk specifically contains critical metadata including width in pixels, height in pixels, bit depth (typically 8 bits per channel), and color type (such as type 2 for RGB without alpha). Each chunk also includes a CRC-32 checksum at the end to detect file corruption.
questions.question: Which of the following is a required chunk in a PNG file format?
questions.explanation: The IHDR chunk is a required first chunk in PNG files that contains essential image metadata such as width, height, bit depth, and color type. The other options (GIF, BMP, TIFF) are different image file formats, not PNG chunks.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG compression pipeline begins with raw image data, which is first processed by Filtering to predict each pixel from its neighbors, storing differences rather than absolute values. After filtering, the LZ77 algorithm scans the data to find repeated patterns and replaces them with compact back‑references, reducing redundancy. Finally, Huffman Encoding assigns short binary codes to the most common values, further shrinking the bit stream. The result is then wrapped in the PNG format to produce a final Compressed PNG file.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the lossless PNG compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: LZ77 Sliding Window in PNG Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression uses clever algorithms to shrink files without losing any data. One key technique is called LZ77, which finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with compact references. According to the content, LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data. Any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of being repeated. This approach helps reduce file size significantly for images with lots of similar regions, like solid backgrounds or gradients.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window that LZ77 maintains when compressing PNG files?

questions.lessonContent: PNG is the preferred format for lossless compression, preserving every single pixel perfectly. It uses three main techniques: filtering (predicting values from neighbors), LZ77 (finding repeated patterns), and Huffman coding (using shorter codes for common values). The content specifically mentions that screenshots with large solid color regions can achieve 10-50x compression using PNG's lossless methods. This makes PNG ideal for graphics with sharp edges like screenshots, text, and diagrams where preserving exact pixel values is critical.
questions.question: PNG lossless compression can achieve 10-50x file size reduction for images with large solid color regions.

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses prediction methods to reduce file size by storing differences between pixels rather than absolute values. The content describes four prediction methods that PNG encoders can use: Sub (predicts from left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predicts from pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predicts from average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal). Each encoder tries each method per row and selects the one that compresses best. These methods exploit the fact that adjacent pixels are usually similar.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method intelligently selects between left, above, or diagonal pixels based on which is closest?
questions.explanation: The Paeth predictor 'smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal' based on which neighbor is closest, making it the most sophisticated prediction method.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since human eyes won't notice the slight color changes. The human visual system resolves brightness in fine detail but blurs color together, meaning you notice blurry edges but don't notice if colors are slightly off. This separation allows JPEG to discard more color information while preserving the brightness details that are more important to perceived image quality.
questions.question: Which transformation does JPEG apply to pixels to separate brightness from color?
questions.answer: Converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression like JPEG can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference. However, with lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back once they are discarded. When you crank up the compression settings, you'll see blocking artifacts where fine details get lost. At high quality settings, you barely notice the difference from the original image. The trade-off involves accepting permanent data loss in exchange for significant file size reduction.
questions.question: In lossy compression like JPEG, once the compressed file is created, it is possible to recover the exact original pixel data.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG processes images by dividing them into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the visual information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What is the block size used by JPEG when dividing an image for compression processing?
questions.explanation: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components for compression.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression uses several key steps to reduce file size while maintaining visual quality. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components using DCT. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components, which JPEG then quantizes to throw away details humans won't notice.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the DCT transformation process used by JPEG?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' which is the origin of the word 'prince.' Additionally, he was made 'Imperator,' meaning 'successful general,' which is the origin of the word 'emperor.' He was also made 'Pontifex Maximus,' or 'chief religious leader, which is the origin of the word 'pontiff' used to describe the pope today.
questions.question: What Latin title given to Augustus means 'successful general' and is the origin of the word 'emperor'?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, resulting in complete control meaning almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship.
questions.question: The Pax Romana, or Roman Peace, lasted for nearly 200 years of relative peace and stability.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Early Roman Emperors and Hereditary Succession
questions.lessonContent: The office of emperor was initially designed to be hereditary, but from the start, there was confusion as to which family member would inherit the throne. Some emperors proved to be cutthroats, or insane, or both. Caligula ruled for two years of good, effective rule, interrupted by a severe illness, followed by two years of horrible rule where he exiled, killed, or forced suicide upon family members and perceived enemies. Nero came to power after his mother allegedly poisoned his predecessor Claudius, and he subsequently murdered his mother, his stepbrother, two of his wives, and his teacher Seneca. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor.
questions.question: Which Roman emperor earned his nickname 'Caligula,' meaning 'little boots,' from the Roman army as a child?
questions.explanation: Caligula earned his name 'Caligula,' meaning 'little boots,' by the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this tumultuous year: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This period illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession in the Roman Empire. The military had come to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, and hereditary succession had proven chaotic and bloody. The Year of the Four Emperors demonstrated how easily the empire could be destabilized during transitions of power.
questions.question: In what year did the Year of the Four Emperors occur, when four emperors ruled in quick succession after Nero's death?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marked the end of the ancient Roman Empire in the West. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, however, continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The division between the Eastern and Western empires had begun when Emperor Diocletian first divided the empire for administrative purposes in 285 CE, and this split deepened after Constantine established Constantinople as the capital city.
questions.question: The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian's Administrative Division of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms: the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire and the Western (Roman) Empire. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east-west split deepened further. The Western Empire would end in 476 CE, while the Eastern Empire would survive until 1453.
questions.question: In what year did Emperor Diocletian first divide the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms?
questions.explanation: Diocletian divided the empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms in 285 CE, which was the first step toward creating two separate empires that would eventually split permanently.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The division of the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western halves was a gradual process that ultimately led to the fall of the Western Empire. First, Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE for more effective administration. Then, Emperor Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming the city Constantinople. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened considerably. These three events represent key milestones in the process of political division that weakened the Western Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the political division of the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History
questions.lessonTitle: Roman Law: Foundation of Modern Legal Systems
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years. It included decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. Roman law was divided into public law (relationship of citizen to state), private or civil law (relationships between people), and peoples law called jus gentium (rights of foreigners). The Justinian Code, or Corpus Juris Civilis, was a comprehensive rewriting of Roman law completed in the 6th century CE that encapsulated the previous over 1000 years of Roman legal development. The Justinian Code still serves as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.
questions.question: What document from the 6th century CE encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law and still serves as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History
questions.lessonContent: A large part of Rome's success was due to the importance Rome placed on building and maintaining the empire's infrastructure. The Romans constructed aqueducts, bridges, dams, harbors, and roads that facilitated movement by officials, soldiers, traders, and travelers throughout the empire. In public architecture, they built amphitheaters such as the Colosseum, basilicas (oblong halls), government offices, palaces, public baths, and theaters. Roman architectural innovations included copying the basic style from the Greeks, adapting the arch from the Etruscans, and developing the dome and vault. The Romans were particularly practical in their engineering approach, prioritizing public health and sanitation through aqueducts that brought fresh water and sewers that carried away dirty water.
questions.question: The Romans copied their basic architectural style from the Greeks and adapted the arch from the Etruscans. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History
questions.lessonContent: The Romance languages developed from Latin and include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. Old English was a Germanic language, but when William the Conqueror of Normandy brought French to England in 1066, it created Middle English, a mixture of Germanic and French languages. Today, about half of modern English can be traced to Latin. Beyond everyday language, Latin also remained important in specialized fields: scientists have traditionally used Latin as a universal language, and our scientific names as well as most legal and medical terminology are derived from Latin. The Catholic Church preserved the Latin language, and Catholic masses were said in Latin until the 1960s.
questions.question: Which of the following languages developed from Latin and is classified as a Romance language?
questions.explanation: French is a Romance language that developed from Latin. German, English, and Swedish are Germanic languages, not Romance languages. The Romance languages (meaning 'Roman') that developed from Latin are French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Roman Contributions to World History
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables (450 BCE), which was the earliest attempt to write down Roman laws for all to see. During the Roman Republic, judicial decisions made by judges added to the body of law. Under the Roman Empire, rulings by emperors became another source of law. Finally, in the 6th century CE, Emperor Justinian compiled and organized all previous Roman laws into the Justinian Code, which still forms the basis for civil law in many countries today.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the development of Roman law?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. Our Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. The system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. This architecture allows for efficient information gathering through parallel execution.
questions.question: According to the content, what is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A system consisting of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage and Performance in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Our analysis found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the two other explanatory factors. Multi-agent architectures effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents by distributing work across agents with separate context windows. In our data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. Multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased token usage.
questions.question: Token usage explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. Our internal evaluations show that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: Based on the internal research evaluation described, what was the performance improvement percentage of the multi-agent system (using Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) compared to single-agent Claude Opus 4?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval.

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). They experimented with multiple judges but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: What scoring range did Anthropic's LLM-as-judge use to evaluate research outputs?

questions.lessonContent: Traditional evaluations often assume that the AI follows the same steps each time: given input X, the system should follow path Y to produce output Z. However, multi-agent systems don't work this way. Even with identical starting points, agents might take completely different valid paths to reach their goal. One agent might search three sources while another searches ten, or they might use different tools to find the same answer. Because we don't always know what the right steps are, we usually can't just check if agents followed the correct steps we prescribed in advance.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems can be effectively evaluated by checking if agents followed pre-prescribed steps in the same way traditional software is tested.

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. This separation provides distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories, which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.'

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation of multi-agent systems requires a phased approach. According to the content, the process begins with small-scale testing using approximately 20 queries representing real usage patterns, where dramatic impacts from changes can be spotted with just a few test cases. Once initial testing shows promising results, LLM-as-judge evaluation is used to scalably evaluate hundreds of outputs by grading outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and citation accuracy. Finally, human evaluation is added to catch edge cases that automation misses, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the evaluation methodology for multi-agent research systems?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems have significant computational costs compared to single-agent approaches. In practice, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than standard chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token consumption is due to parallel processing across multiple subagents, each operating with their own context windows. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value is high enough to pay for the increased performance. Some domains requiring all agents to share the same context or involving many dependencies between agents are not a good fit for multi-agent systems today.
questions.question: According to the content, how many times more tokens do multi-agent systems use compared to standard chat interactions?

questions.lessonContent: Debugging multi-agent systems requires different approaches than traditional software due to the dynamic and non-deterministic nature of agent decisions. Users would report agents not finding obvious information, but the root cause was difficult to diagnose. The challenges included determining whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. Adding full production tracing allowed the team to diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, they monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents, maintaining user privacy while still diagnosing root causes.
questions.question: Production tracing enables developers to diagnose why agents failed without monitoring individual conversation contents.

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process, meaning well-meaning code changes could break existing agents. The team cannot update every agent to the new version simultaneously. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This approach ensures that agents currently executing tasks are not interrupted and can complete their work with the original configuration.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to avoid disrupting running agents during updates?
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, avoiding disruption to agents that might be in the middle of executing tasks.

questions.lessonContent: When deploying updates to agent systems, careful coordination is required because agents might be anywhere in their process when updates occur. To prevent code changes from breaking running agents, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments. This involves initiating the deployment while keeping both old and new versions running simultaneously, then gradually shifting traffic from the old version to the new version while monitoring for any issues, and finally completing the full rollout once the new version is verified as working correctly.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the rainbow deployment process for multi-agent systems?

It offers 8 leading embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models. These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models that support different context lengths. These models include versions with 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.

According to the release announcement, users can access these powerful models at prices that are up to 4 times cheaper than other popular platforms, as illustrated in the pricing graph included in the original announcement. questions.lessonTitle: Vector Databases Compatible with Together Embeddings for RAG
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These vector databases store the embeddings generated from the Together Embeddings endpoint and enable efficient similarity search for retrieval. Additionally, you can leverage frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex to build RAG applications more easily. The Together platform provides deep-dive tutorials for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex.
questions.question: Which three vector databases are mentioned as compatible for building RAG applications with Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonContent: Building RAG applications with Together Embeddings is streamlined through integration with popular frameworks. The content specifically mentions that you can leverage frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to build RAG applications. These frameworks provide built-in components for handling document loading, text splitting, embedding generation, vector storage, and retrieval pipelines. This makes it easier for developers to implement RAG without building each component from scratch.
questions.question: You can build RAG applications with Together using LangChain and LlamaIndex frameworks.

questions.lessonContent: The Together platform provides multiple approaches for implementing Retrieval Augmented Generation. Developers can build RAG using the Together API combined with vector databases like MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma for storing and retrieving embeddings. Alternatively, developers can use frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex which offer streamlined RAG implementations. The platform offers dedicated tutorials for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, as well as with LangChain and LlamaIndex, making it accessible for developers with different technical backgrounds and preferences.

choices: Using only OpenAI and Anthropic APIs
Using vector databases (MongoDB, Pinecone, Chroma) or frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex)
