Claudius became emperor because he was the last adult male of his family, brought southern Britannia under Roman control, and conducted a census in 48 CE. Nero, considered a tyrant, came to power after his mother allegedly poisoned his predecessor Claudius, and murdered his mother, stepbrother, two wives, and his teacher Seneca; he was accused of starting the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE and blamed Christians for it before being forced to commit suicide.
questions.question: Which emperor was accused of setting the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE and blamed Christians for it?
questions.explanation: Nero was accused of setting the fire in Rome in 64 CE and of fiddling while the city burned. He blamed the fire on the new religious group known as "Christians" and was ultimately forced to commit suicide.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: From Republic to Imperial Rule
questions.lessonTitle: From Republic to Empire: The Rise of Augustus
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name Augustus, meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Octavian (now referred to as Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power as Augustus?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Pax Romana and Imperial Successors
questions.lessonTitle: The Pax Romana: Definition and Duration
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, which means "Roman Peace," describes the period when Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond. Complete Roman control meant almost no warfare within the empire's borders. This remarkable peace lasted nearly 200 years, from approximately 27 BCE to 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship, integrating diverse populations into the Roman system.
questions.question: What was the Pax Romana and approximately how long did it last?
questions.answer: The Pax Romana was the period of Roman peace and control of the Mediterranean region that lasted nearly 200 years

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Pax Romana and Imperial Successors
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After the death of Emperor Nero in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this period: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This rapid succession of rulers illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession that plagued the Roman Empire. The military played an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor during this chaotic time.
questions.question: The Year of the Four Emperors was a period of stability and orderly succession in the Roman Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Pax Romana and Imperial Successors
questions.lessonContent: Vespasian became emperor in 69 CE and is best known for building the Colosseum in Rome, where gladiatorial combats were held. He also oversaw the First Jewish Revolt (66-70 CE), during which the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed in the Roman province of Judea. This destruction was carried out by Vespasian's son, Titus, and marked the end of the Second Temple period. Vespasian was succeeded first by his son Titus, and then by his other son Domitian.
questions.question: Which of the following is associated with Emperor Vespasian?
choices: Expanding the empire to its greatest extent
questions.explanation: Vespasian is specifically associated with building the Colosseum in Rome, where gladiatorial contests were held. Trajan oversaw the empire's greatest extent, Hadrian built Hadrian's Wall, and Claudius conquered southern Britannia.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Pax Romana and Imperial Successors
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. First, Galba became emperor after being declared so by the Senate. However, Otho then overthrows Galba in a power struggle, having his predecessor murdered. Shortly after, Vitellius defeats Otho in battle near Bedriacum, forcing Otho to commit suicide. Vespasian would later defeat Vitellius and establish a new dynasty.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Transformation and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This marked the culmination of a century of chaos following the death of Marcus Aurelius, known as the Crisis of the Third Century. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The empire had experienced significant internal divisions, with Diocletian first dividing the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, and Constantine further deepening this split by establishing Constantinople as the capital.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Transformation and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The decline of the Roman Empire had several economic causes that weakened the empire over time. There was a significant gap between the rich and the poor, which created social tension. Impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni and were sold along with the land they worked. As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to buy goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined. Additionally, large estates became self-sufficient, further hurting manufacturing and trade throughout the empire.
questions.question: The economic decline of the Roman Empire was caused by increasing wealth equality and growing manufacturing trade.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Transformation and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. The law encompassed several branches: public law governed the relationship of citizen to state, private (civil) law governed relationships between people, and peoples law (jus gentium) covered the rights of foreigners. In the 6th century CE, Emperor Justinian rewrote Roman law in what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis or the Justinian Code. This compilation encapsulated the previous thousand years of Roman law and still serves as the basis for civil law in many countries in Europe today.
questions.question: Which of the following represents the origin of Roman law?
questions.explanation: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE, which were the first written laws of the Roman Republic.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Transformation and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Division and Transformation of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After centuries of expansion and relative stability, the Roman Empire faced significant challenges that led to its transformation. Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE as the first step in creating what would become separate empires. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople, which deepened the east-west split. The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed, while the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the division and transformation of the Roman Empire?
choices: Constantine moves the capital from Rome to Constantinople
Diocletian divides the empire into east and west administrative realms
The Western Roman Empire ends in 476 CE

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: What is a Multi-Agent Research System
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish tasks. Our Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously.
questions.question: What type of architecture does Anthropic's Research system use to coordinate its agents?

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Agent Systems Excel at Breadth-First Research
questions.lessonContent: Research work involves open-ended problems where it's very difficult to predict the required steps in advance, making AI agents particularly well-suited for these tasks. Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all the board members of the companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found the correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed to find the answer with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems are particularly effective for breadth-first queries that pursue multiple independent directions simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation. We found that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates our architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The latest Claude models act as large efficiency multipliers on token use, as upgrading to Claude Sonnet 4 is a larger performance gain than doubling the token budget on Claude Sonnet 3.7. Multi-agent architectures effectively scale token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents.
questions.question: Which factor explains the largest portion of performance variance in multi-agent research systems?
questions.explanation: According to Anthropic's analysis, token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance, making it the dominant factor. The number of tool calls and model choice are the two other explanatory factors but account for less variance combined.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Research Effort to Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent research systems, agents often struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks. Anthropic embedded scaling rules directly into their prompts to address this challenge. Simple fact-finding tasks require just one agent with three to ten tool calls, while direct comparisons might need two to four subagents with ten to fifteen calls each. Complex research scenarios can use more than ten subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was identified as a common failure mode in early system versions.
questions.question: According to the prompt engineering principles, how many subagents with clearly divided responsibilities are recommended for complex research tasks?

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic uses LLM-as-judge evaluation to scale the assessment of research outputs, which are free-form text that rarely have a single correct answer. Their LLM judge evaluates outputs against a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They found that a single LLM call with one prompt outputting scores from 0.0 to 1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent method and aligned well with human judgements. This evaluation approach is especially effective when test cases have clear answers, such as accurately listing companies with the top three largest R&D budgets.
questions.question: LLM-as-judge evaluation using a single LLM call that outputs scores from 0.0 to 1.0 and a pass-fail grade produces results that are inconsistent with human judgements.

questions.lessonContent: Tool design and selection are critical to agent performance because agent-tool interfaces function like human-computer interfaces. Using the correct tool is often strictly necessary for task success—for example, an agent searching the web for context that only exists in Slack is doomed from the start. Anthropic gave their agents explicit heuristics to handle this: first, examine all available tools before use; second, match tool usage to user intent; third, search the web for broad external exploration; fourth, prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description to prevent failures.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an explicit heuristic that Anthropic's agents are given for tool selection and use?
choices: Match tool usage to user intent
Search the web for broad external exploration
Examine all available tools first before use
Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage' because the content explicitly states the opposite: agents should 'prefer specialized tools over generic ones.' The other three options (examine all tools first, match to user intent, search the web for exploration) are all stated as explicit heuristics in the content.

questions.lessonTitle: Agent State Management and Error Handling
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means we need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, we cannot just restart from the beginning because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, we built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. We also use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully: for instance, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt works surprisingly well. We combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What two approaches does Anthropic combine to handle errors gracefully in their agent systems?
questions.answer: They combine the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts. This makes debugging harder. For instance, users would report agents not finding obvious information, but we could not see why. Were the agents using bad search queries? Choosing poor sources? Hitting tool failures? Adding full production tracing let us diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically. Beyond standard observability, we monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures, all without monitoring the contents of individual conversations to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped us diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: True or False: In Anthropic's production tracing for agents, they monitor the contents of individual conversations to diagnose failures.

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever we deploy updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. We therefore need to prevent our well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. We cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, we use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to avoid disrupting running agents during updates?
choices: Rolling deployments that restart each agent individually with the new version
Canary deployments that route a small percentage of traffic to the new version
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running
Blue-green deployments that instantly switch all traffic to the new version
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: In Anthropic's multi-agent research system, the workflow begins when a user submits a query. The lead agent then plans the research strategy and creates specialized subagents to explore different aspects of the query. These subagents perform parallel searches, returning their findings which are then synthesized by the lead agent before the system checks research quality and processes citations.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research workflow from initial query to final results?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, offering developers access to 8 leading open-source embedding models. These models include top performers from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models. The M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The 32k model represents the longest context option, enabling embeddings for very large documents.
questions.question: What is the maximum context length available for M2-BERT retrieval models in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT retrieval models in the Together Embeddings endpoint are specifically designed for long context tasks and significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval benchmarks. These models allow users to generate embeddings for long documents without needing to split them into many short chunks, while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. This capability addresses a common challenge where earlier models could only process shorter text segments effectively.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models require documents to be split into many short chunks before generating embeddings.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings provides access to powerful embedding models at very competitive prices compared to other platforms. The pricing structure shows that Together Embeddings is up to 4x cheaper than other popular embedding platforms. This cost advantage makes it accessible for developers and organizations building AI applications at scale, while still delivering state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like MTEB.
questions.question: According to the content, how many times cheaper is Together Embeddings compared to other popular platforms?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Together Embeddings is 'up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms' as seen in the pricing graph mentioned in the release announcement.

questions.lessonContent: To visualize sample data using the Together Embeddings endpoint, you first extract text samples from a data file. Next, you generate embeddings for these text samples using the Together API. Finally, you transform the embedding vectors with tSNE to reduce their dimensionality for 2D visualization.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings data visualization process?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is designed with full OpenAI API compatibility. This means developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API can easily switch to Together's endpoint by changing only the base URL and API key. The endpoint supports the same input format and response structure as OpenAI's embeddings API, minimizing the code changes required for migration. This compatibility feature lowers the barrier for developers to try Together's potentially better performing models.
questions.question: What feature of the Together Embeddings endpoint makes it easy to migrate applications already built with the OpenAI API?

questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint, models are specified using a specific API string format. The API string contains the organization name followed by a slash and the model name with its specifications. For example, the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model is referenced as 'togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval'. This same format pattern is used for other models like the 32k variant which uses 'togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval'. The API string is passed as a parameter when calling the embeddings.create() method.
questions.question: The API string 'togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval' is the correct format for specifying the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model in the Together Embeddings endpoint.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint launched with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k. The M2-BERT retrieval models are specifically designed for long context retrieval tasks and can handle longer documents without requiring them to be split into many short chunks. Users can select different models depending on their needs for context length and performance.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid model option available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval' as this is explicitly listed in the content as the API string for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model. The other options are not mentioned in the source content - while OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 are mentioned as benchmarks for comparison, they are not available as model options in the Together endpoint.

questions.lessonContent: When working with embeddings for data visualization, it's important to understand that embedding vectors typically have dimensions that are too large to easily visualize in their raw form. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model available in the Together Embeddings endpoint, the embedding dimension is 768. This means each text sample is represented as a vector of 768 numbers. To plot each data example in a 2D space for visualization, we must use dimensionality reduction techniques such as tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform these high-dimensional vectors into a format suitable for plotting.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?

questions.lessonContent: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model. Building a RAG system using the Together API involves using embeddings to represent documents and then retrieving the most relevant ones based on similarity. The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integration with popular vector databases and frameworks for this purpose.
questions.question: RAG systems work by finding relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and providing that information to a generative model.

questions.lessonContent: The Together blog demonstrates data visualization using embeddings from the RedPajama-v1 Sample dataset. In the example provided, the visualization code processes four different data sources: arxiv_sample.jsonl containing academic papers, book_sample.jsonl containing book text, c4_sample.jsonl containing web text, and github_sample.jsonl containing code. When plotted using tSNE with a perplexity of 15, texts from each data source appear somewhat closely located, showing that the embedding model successfully captures the semantic differences between domains. The visualization also shows similarities between github and stackexchange data, and between book and c4 data.
questions.question: From which file is the wikipedia_sample.jsonl data in the visualization example?
questions.explanation: The visualization example uses arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, and github_sample.jsonl. Wikipedia_sample.jsonl is not among the files used in the visualization code shown in the source content.

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations: Composer 2 Overview and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonTitle: Composer 2 Model Overview and Training Phases
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering that demonstrates strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. The model is trained in two distinct phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch. The model scores strongly on CursorBench, the team's internal benchmark of real-world software engineering, while also scoring at frontier levels on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench.
questions.question: In what two phases is Composer 2 trained?
questions.answer: Continued pretraining followed by large-scale reinforcement learning

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations: Composer 2 Overview and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. The team used internal evaluations and inference performance considerations to select a base model, measuring internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking. These evaluations led them to select Kimi K2.5, a 1.04T parameter / 32B active parameter Mixture-of-Experts model as the base model for Composer 2. They extend Kimi K2.5 with a continued pretraining stage on a large code-dominated data mix to provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities.
questions.question: Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 1.04T total parameters and 32B active parameters. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations: Composer 2 Overview and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonTitle: Continued Pretraining Phases and Multi-Token Prediction
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage is divided into three phases: the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks. To serve the model faster in production, the team trains additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers to use with speculative decoding. They initialize the MTP layers from scratch and train them on the same data mix, using self-distillation to speed up convergence by teaching the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position. The MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run and are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model during the final two phases.
questions.question: What are the three phases of continued pretraining for Composer 2?
choices: Base model training, agentic training, and evaluation training
Short context training, medium context training, and long context training
Initial pretraining, intermediate fine-tuning, and final RL training
Bulk compute at 32k token length, long-context extension to 256k, and short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states the three phases: spending the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, followed by a shorter long-context extension phase to 256k sequence length, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning: Training Methodology and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to incentivize quick solutions on easy requests while allowing more thinking time on hard requests. The penalty formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = (1 + kx)1−q −1 / (k(1 −q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining curvature. The input x is not a simple measure but rather a weighted combination of multiple token types and counts: thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, the number of tool calls, and the number of turns in a rollout. This composite measure allows the model to learn efficient behaviors, such as making multiple tool calls in parallel, because the penalty reflects that on easy tasks achievable with few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks.
questions.question: According to the content, what specific components are combined to form the input x in the nonlinear length penalty formula?
questions.answer: thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning: Training Methodology and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning training operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. The training uses a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt in a single-epoch regime where the same prompt is never trained on twice. In their experiments with various policy gradient variants, they examined whether to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length. Some prior works employed overlong masking while others found mixed results—Liu et al. found it showed limited effectiveness on long-tail reasoning tasks but increased accuracy in medium and short-length reasoning tasks, while Du et al. found it caused output length to grow too quickly. Based on their own experiments at small scale, the Composer 2 team did not see benefits with overlong masking and chose not to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length.
questions.question: Composer 2's RL training uses overlong masking to handle rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning: Training Methodology and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons in software engineering tasks, the model uses a technique called self-summarization that was introduced in Composer 1.5. This technique allows each training rollout to involve multiple generations chained together by summaries rather than being limited to a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and the self-summarizations that made them work. At the same time, poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information even with a limited context window, and for hard examples it often self-summarizes multiple times. Experiments show that self-summarization consistently reduces error compared to using separate prompt-based compaction while using significantly fewer tokens and reusing the KV cache.
questions.question: What technique does Composer 2 use to enable working across long horizons?
questions.explanation: Self-summarization, introduced in Composer 1.5, allows multiple generations to be chained together by summaries rather than a single prompt-response pair. This enables the model to process more information across long horizons while using fewer tokens.

questions.moduleTitle: Reinforcement Learning: Training Methodology and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: In the reinforcement learning pipeline for Composer 2, the process begins by sampling a problem from a distribution that reflects common coding use cases. The agent then generates rollouts by executing actions in the environment, producing sequences of tool calls and responses. After rollout generation, the system calculates various token counts including thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, and final message tokens. These token counts are then used to apply a nonlinear length penalty that incentivizes the model to respond quickly on easy tasks while allowing more thinking time on complex problems. Finally, the nonlinear length penalty is combined with correctness rewards to compute the final reward, which is used to update model weights via policy gradient.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the reward computation process for Composer 2's reinforcement learning training?

questions.moduleTitle: Evaluation and Infrastructure: Benchmarks, Results, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite designed to reflect real-world software engineering tasks. Compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed versus just 7-10 lines for those public benchmarks. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters, compared to 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks, according to the content?

questions.moduleTitle: Evaluation and Infrastructure: Benchmarks, Results, and System Architecture
questions.lessonTitle: Quantization Format for MoE Backward Pass
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats, targeting NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for block-scaled tensor-core matrix multiplications. For the MoE backward pass, the standard MXFP8 format is used with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. The forward pass uses NVFP4 to match inference for numerical stability, while the backward pass runs only on the training cluster and can afford higher precision to improve training stability. The choice of hardware-level math precision matters considerably for training convergence.
questions.question: The MoE backward pass uses the standard MXFP8 format with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Evaluation and Infrastructure: Benchmarks, Results, and System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services that enable large-scale global training with high availability and independent scaling. These services are: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. This decoupled service architecture allows training to be more resilient to failures in individual services, and enables independent scaling and sharding of different components.
questions.question: According to the content, what are the four services that make up Composer 2's RL infrastructure?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'Our RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations.'

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Configuring Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, and developer environment setup. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude (most useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all your claude sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: In which location can a CLAUDE.md file be placed so that it applies to all Claude Code sessions regardless of directory?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Configuring Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Configuring Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, or using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: The /permissions command can be used to add or remove tools from the allowed tools list.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Configuring Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: MCP Server Configuration in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, connecting to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. There are three primary ways to configure MCP connections for your projects. You can configure MCP servers in your project config, which makes them available when running Claude Code in that specific directory. You can also configure them in your global config, which makes them available in all projects. Additionally, you can check in a .mcp.json file into your repository, which makes those MCP servers available to anyone working on your codebase. For example, you could add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json so that every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box.
questions.question: What are the three ways to configure MCP servers in Claude Code?
choices: Only through CLI flags and settings.json
Only project config and global config
Project config, global config, and .mcp.json file
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that MCP servers can be configured in project config, global config, or a checked-in .mcp.json file.

questions.lessonTitle: Thinking Budget Levels in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, using specific phrases triggers extended thinking mode with progressively higher thinking budgets. The phrase 'think' provides additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. These specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system: 'think' is the baseline, followed by 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink' at the highest level. Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use. This extended thinking mode gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly before responding.
questions.question: What is the order of thinking budget phrases from lowest to highest in Claude Code?
questions.answer: think < think hard < think harder < ultrathink

questions.lessonTitle: Codebase Q&A Requires No Special Prompting
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can agentically search the codebase to answer general questions about your code during onboarding. When using Claude for learning and exploration on a new codebase, you can ask Claude the same sorts of questions you would ask another engineer on the project when pair programming. Questions can range from 'How does logging work?' to 'What does async move { ... } do on line 134 of foo.rs?' At Anthropic, using Claude Code in this way has become their core onboarding workflow. The content explicitly states that no special prompting is required for this workflow.
questions.question: True or False: Using Claude Code for codebase Q&A requires special prompting or instructions.

questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Passing Data to Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Several methods exist for providing data to Claude during a session. The most common approach is to copy and paste data directly into your prompt. Another method is piping data into Claude Code using command line syntax like 'cat foo.txt | claude', which is particularly useful for logs, CSVs, and large data files. You can also tell Claude to pull data via bash commands, MCP tools, or custom slash commands. Additionally, you can ask Claude to read files or fetch URLs, which also works for images. Most sessions involve a combination of these approaches.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a method for passing data into Claude Code?
choices: Pipe into Claude Code (e.g., cat foo.txt | claude)
Copy and paste directly into your prompt
Tell Claude to pull data via bash commands, MCP tools, or custom slash commands
questions.explanation: The source explicitly mentions copy/paste, piping with 'cat', and pulling via bash/MCP/slash commands. Voice dictation is not mentioned anywhere in the content.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Usage and Multi-Claude Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, use the -p flag followed by your prompt. For streaming JSON output, you can combine -p with the --output-format stream-json flag. It is important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you must trigger it each time you start a new session. The --verbose flag can also be helpful for debugging Claude invocations during development.
questions.question: What flag is used to enable headless mode in Claude Code for non-interactive contexts?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Usage and Multi-Claude Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. This enables running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, with each instance focused on its own independent task. Since the tasks don't overlap in different worktrees, each Claude can work at full speed without waiting for the other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts. When finished, you can clean up a worktree using the git worktree remove command.
questions.question: True or False: Multiple Claude instances can work simultaneously on different git worktrees of the same repository without merge conflicts.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Advanced Usage and Multi-Claude Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Headless mode with the -p flag integrates Claude Code programmatically into larger workflows while leveraging its built-in tools and system prompt. There are two primary patterns for this integration. The first is fanning out, which handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude generate a task list and then looping through tasks, calling Claude programmatically for each with specific instructions and allowed tools. The second pattern is pipelining, which integrates Claude into existing data or processing pipelines by calling claude -p with a prompt and piping the JSON output to the next command in your processing pipeline.
questions.question: Which of the following is a primary pattern for programmatically integrating Claude Code using headless mode?
choices: Fanning out to handle large-scale migrations or analyses
Using the /clear command to reset context
Running multiple checkouts in separate folders
questions.explanation: Fanning out is explicitly listed as one of the two primary patterns for using headless mode, involving generating a task list and looping through tasks with programmatic Claude calls.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but when you zoom in far enough, you'll see they are made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. Each of these color values ranges from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, meaning maximum intensity of that color. For example, the RGB values (255, 147, 41) create a bright orange color. Together, these three values determine every visible color in a digital image.
questions.question: What are the three color values that each pixel contains?

questions.lessonContent: An HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million individual pixels. Specifically, 1,920 multiplied by 1,080 equals 2,073,600 pixels. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes of data (one byte each for red, green, and blue), the total raw file size is 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes, approximately 6.2 megabytes. This is why image compression is essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently over the internet.
questions.question: A 1920 × 1080 pixel image with 3 bytes per pixel has an uncompressed size of approximately 6.2 MB.

questions.lessonContent: Image compression uses two fundamental approaches to reduce file size. The first approach, called lossy compression, throws away data that humans won't notice, such as subtle color variations, which allows for 10-20x smaller files. The second approach, called lossless compression, keeps every pixel perfect by being clever about how data is stored, using techniques like predicting values from neighboring pixels and finding repeated patterns. Lossless compression typically achieves 3-10x smaller files without any loss in quality. JPEG uses lossy compression, while PNG uses lossless compression.
questions.question: Which compression approach keeps every pixel perfect while still reducing file size?
questions.explanation: Lossless compression preserves every single pixel while shrinking the file, as stated in the content about PNG.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG lossless compression pipeline begins by applying filtering to each row of the image, storing differences between adjacent pixels rather than raw values. After filtering, the LZ77 algorithm scans the data for repeated patterns and replaces them with back‑references to reduce redundancy. Finally, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to the most frequently occurring values, further shrinking the bit stream. This three‑step sequence is what makes PNG able to compress images without losing any pixel information. The process is repeated for every row of the image to maximize compression efficiency.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Size in Lossy Compression
questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact. This block-based transformation is a fundamental part of how JPEG achieves compression.
questions.question: What is the size of each pixel block that JPEG divides the image into?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works, as eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. JPEG takes advantage of this by reducing color resolution since your eyes won't notice. It throws away high-frequency details that represent fine details like sharp edges, keeping the smooth parts intact. With lossy compression, you can't get the original pixels back because the data has been permanently discarded. The tradeoff is often worth it: 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference.
questions.question: With lossy compression, you cannot recover the original pixel data because it has been permanently discarded.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG is a lossy compression format used by cameras and photographs. It converts pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution to achieve compression. However, JPEG doesn't support alpha (transparency). PNG, which uses lossless compression, supports alpha and is preferred for graphics with transparency. This is one key reason why PNG is chosen over JPEG for images that need transparent backgrounds.
questions.question: Which format supports alpha (transparency) for images?
questions.explanation: JPEG does not support alpha transparency, while PNG does support it. This is explicitly stated as one reason PNG is preferred for graphics with transparency.

questions.lessonContent: In lossy JPEG compression, after the image is prepared through color space conversion and color resolution reduction, the next critical steps involve processing 8x8 pixel blocks. Each block undergoes a mathematical transformation that converts spatial pixel data into frequency components. This transformation separates smooth gradient information (low frequencies) from sharp detail information (high frequencies). The compression algorithm then selectively discards the high-frequency components that contain fine details, since human vision is less sensitive to these nuances.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in JPEG's frequency-based compression?

questions.lessonContent: The third trick in lossless compression involves finding repeated patterns using an algorithm called LZ77. This algorithm maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of processed data. When LZ77 detects a pattern that has appeared within this 32 KB window, it replaces the repeated sequence with a back-reference indicating how far back to look and how many bytes to copy. This approach is particularly effective for images with large solid color regions or gradual gradients, as repeated patterns can be referenced multiple times instead of storing the full data repeatedly.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window that LZ77 uses when finding repeated patterns?

questions.lessonContent: PNG files include error detection mechanisms to handle potential data corruption from network issues or buggy programs. Each chunk in a PNG file contains a mathematical fingerprint known as a CRC-32 checksum. When you open a PNG file, your computer recalculates this fingerprint and compares it against the stored value. If the checksums don't match, the file is considered damaged and won't be displayed properly.
questions.question: PNG detects file corruption using mathematical fingerprints in each chunk called CRC-32 checksums.

questions.lessonContent: When all the compressed data is ready, it gets wrapped in a structured PNG file format organized into chunks with specific purposes. The most important chunks are: IHDR (Image Header) which contains metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type; IDAT (Image Data) which contains the actual compressed pixel data; and IEND (Image End) which marks the end of the file. The IHDR chunk must appear first and includes details like whether the image uses RGB or RGBA (which supports transparency).
questions.question: Which of the following are the three required chunks in a PNG file format?
questions.explanation: The PNG format requires three specific chunks: IHDR (Image Header with metadata), IDAT (Image Data with compressed pixels), and IEND (Image End marker). These chunks are essential for proper image decoding.

questions.lessonTitle: Lossless Compression: Pattern Recognition and Replacement
questions.lessonContent: In lossless compression, after the filtering step stores pixel differences, the compression proceeds to identify and handle repeated patterns. The LZ77 algorithm scans through the data looking for sequences that have appeared before within a sliding window. When a repeated pattern is found, instead of storing the full sequence again, the algorithm replaces it with a compact back-reference indicating how far back to look and how many bytes to copy. This approach significantly reduces file size for images with many similar regions like solid colors or gradients.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in LZ77's pattern replacement process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Structure of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Dates of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: There were two periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, but the term Roman Empire specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors. The transition from Republic to Empire occurred when Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Structure of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Meaning of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase primus inter pares means first among equals. Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being first among equals gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else.
questions.question: The Latin phrase primus inter pares refers to the idea that Roman emperors were simply 'first among equals' with senators, with no real power advantage.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Structure of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After Augustus, there was great variety in the quality of emperors who ruled Rome. The office of emperor was initially designed to be hereditary, but from the start there was confusion as to which family member would inherit the throne. Some emperors proved to be cutthroats, or insane, or both. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor. Caligula, who ruled from 37 CE to 41 CE, earned his nickname meaning little boots from the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier. After two years of effective rule, his reign was marked by horrible atrocities including exiling, killing, and forcing family members to commit suicide. He was assassinated in 41 CE by members of the Praetorian Guard.
questions.question: Which of the following describes how Caligula received his nickname?
choices: He wore little boots in battle as a military tradition
He collected small boots as a hobby
He was dressed like a soldier by the Roman army as a child, earning the name 'little boots'
He was given tiny boots as a gift from his father Germanicus
questions.explanation: Caligula earned his name 'Caligula,' meaning 'little boots,' by the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Structure of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Rise and Structure of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. Following this victory, the Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." Then, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate, solidifying his political power.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this chaotic period: Galba first, then Otho, followed by Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This rapid succession of rulers demonstrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession that plagued the Roman Empire. The military played an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor, and the lack of a clear hereditary succession system led to violence and instability.
questions.question: Who was the fourth and final emperor to rule during the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence that had plagued Rome following the death of Marcus Aurelius. In 285 CE, Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms, creating an Eastern and Western division. This was the first step in creating what would eventually become two separate empires: the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen it.
questions.question: Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE to strengthen administrative control.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Constantine became emperor in 312 CE and moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming the city Constantinople (modern Istanbul). His mother Helena had converted to Christianity, and in 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. Constantine ultimately converted to Christianity on his deathbed. This relationship between Constantine and Christianity fundamentally changed the status of the religion in the Roman Empire.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Constantine's relationship with Christianity?
choices: He made Christianity the official religion of Rome immediately upon becoming emperor
He issued the Edict of Milan legalizing Christianity and converted on his deathbed
He was born a Christian and forced all Romans to convert
He banned Christianity and persecuted Christians throughout his reign
questions.explanation: The Edict of Milan in 313 CE legalized Christianity, and Constantine converted to Christianity only on his deathbed. He did not make Christianity the official religion immediately, nor was he born Christian, nor did he persecute Christians.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation and Division of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero committed suicide in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. First, Galba became emperor after Nero's death. Then, Otho replaced Galba when the Senate ordered Galba's execution. Next, Vitellius over threw Otho in another power struggle. Finally, Vespasian defeated Vitellius and established a new dynasty, becoming emperor in 69 CE.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE, Rome experienced a century of chaos known as the Crisis of the Third Century. Diocletian became the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence. The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian leader named Odoacer. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. Odoacer was a Germanic chieftain who ruled Italy after overthrowing the last Western Roman emperor.
questions.question: Who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476 CE?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire faced significant economic decline before its final fall. A growing gap developed between the rich and poor, with impoverished workers becoming tied to the land as coloni who were sold along with the land they worked. As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to purchase goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined substantially. Large estates became increasingly self-sufficient, further hurting manufacturing and trade throughout the empire.
questions.question: As fewer members of the lower classes could afford to buy goods due to lack of purchasing power, manufacturing and trade declined.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Justinian was a powerful emperor of the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire who ruled from 527 to 565 CE and was headquartered at Constantinople. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan who became a powerful co-ruler. Justinian managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last. His most significant accomplishment was rewriting Roman law into what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This legal code encapsulated over a thousand years of Roman legal development and still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes Emperor Justinian's most lasting contribution to world history?
choices: He established Christianity as the official religion of the Roman Empire.
He rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code), which became the basis for civil law in many European countries.
He built the Colosseum in Rome for gladiatorial contests.
He reunited the Eastern and Western empires, which remained united permanently.
questions.explanation: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis encapsulated over 1,000 years of Roman law and remains the basis for civil law systems in many countries today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: The spread of Christianity through the Roman Empire was a gradual process enabled by Roman political and administrative systems. First, Jesus, the founder of Christianity, was born in the Roman province of Judea during the reign of Augustus. Later, according to tradition, Paul of Tarsus (St. Paul) used his Roman citizenship to have his criminal trial relocated to Rome from Caesarea in the 60s CE. Finally, Christianity gained official acceptance with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized the religion, and Constantine's subsequent conversion.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the early spread of Christianity through the Roman Empire?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Definition and Core Components of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature developed by Anthropic uses this architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different facets of the question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. This separation of concerns provides distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories, which reduces path dependency and enables thorough, independent investigations.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A system consisting of multiple LLM agents that autonomously use tools in a loop while working together

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Explains Performance Variance in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems work mainly because they help spend enough tokens to solve the problem. In Anthropic's analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance when testing browsing agents' ability to locate hard-to-find information. Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates the multi-agent architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. However, there is a downside: in practice, these architectures burn through tokens fast, with multi-agent systems using about 15× more tokens than standard chat interactions.
questions.question: Token usage explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.

questions.lessonTitle: Lead Agent Role in Research System Architecture
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a LeadResearcher agent that enters an iterative research process. When processing a query, the LeadResearcher begins by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist the context, since if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated and it is important to retain the plan. It then creates specialized Subagents with specific research tasks, where each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the LeadResearcher. The LeadResearcher synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed—if so, it can create additional subagents or refine its strategy. Once sufficient information is gathered, the system exits the research loop and passes all findings to a CitationAgent, which processes the documents and research report to identify specific locations for citations.
questions.question: What is the role of the LeadResearcher agent in the multi-agent research system?
choices: Coordinates all subagents synchronously so they cannot work in parallel
Acts as a filter that blocks irrelevant information before passing queries to subagents
Analyzes queries, develops strategies, spawns subagents to explore different aspects, and synthesizes findings from subagents
Only searches the web for information and returns results directly to users
questions.explanation: The LeadResearcher analyzes queries, develops strategies, spawns specialized subagents to explore different aspects in parallel, synthesizes their findings, and decides whether more research is needed before passing results to the CitationAgent.

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. This architecture enables parallel processing of complex research tasks that would be impossible for a single agent to handle efficiently.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does the Anthropic Research system use?

questions.lessonTitle: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Execution in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Currently, the lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: The Research system executes subagents asynchronously, allowing the lead agent to steer subagents in real-time.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Comparison Across System Types
questions.lessonContent: Token usage is a critical factor in multi-agent system economics. In their analysis, Anthropic found that agents typically use about 4× more tokens than standard chat interactions. Furthermore, multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats due to the parallel operation of multiple subagents with their own context windows. For economic viability, multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance.
questions.question: How many times more tokens do multi-agent systems use compared to standard chat interactions?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, while single agents use about 4× more tokens than chats.

questions.lessonTitle: Debugging Multi-Agent Systems with Production Tracing
questions.lessonContent: Debugging multi-agent systems requires different approaches than traditional software due to their non-deterministic nature. Even with identical prompts, agents can take completely different paths to reach their goals, making it difficult to diagnose failures. Users would report agents not finding obvious information, but the underlying causes could be varied: agents using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. To diagnose these issues, Anthropic added full production tracing that let them see why agents failed and fix issues systematically. They monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped them diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: What debugging approach did Anthropic implement to diagnose why agents failed?
questions.answer: Full production tracing that monitors agent decision patterns and interaction structures

questions.lessonTitle: Rainbow Deployments Prevent Disruption in Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their research process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents if all agents were updated to the new version simultaneously. To prevent this disruption, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This ensures that agents currently running in production can complete their tasks without interruption while new traffic flows to the updated version.
questions.question: Rainbow deployments update all agent instances to the new version at the exact same time.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort to Query Complexity in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's prompt engineering includes explicit scaling rules to help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently for different query complexities. Simple fact-finding requires just one agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These guidelines prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions where agents would spawn 50 subagents for simple queries. The lead agent analyzes the query, develops a strategy, and determines how many specialized subagents to create based on the estimated complexity of the task.
questions.question: According to Anthropic's scaling rules, how many subagents and tool calls does complex research typically require?
choices: Exactly 5 subagents with 20 tool calls each
More than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities
questions.explanation: Complex research tasks require more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities according to Anthropic's explicit scaling rules embedded in their prompts.

questions.lessonTitle: Prompt Engineering Principles for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: When developing prompts for multi-agent research systems, engineers follow a systematic approach. First, they build simulations using exact prompts and tools to observe agent behavior step-by-step and identify failure modes. Second, they teach the lead agent how to delegate by decomposing queries into subtasks with clear objectives and task boundaries. Third, they implement scaling rules that adjust effort based on query complexity—simple fact-finding requires fewer subagents while complex research needs more specialized agents with clearly divided responsibilities.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the prompt engineering process for multi-agent systems?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers significant cost savings compared to other popular embedding platforms. According to the release announcement, these models can be accessed at very competitive prices, up to 4x cheaper than other platforms. This pricing advantage makes it more accessible for developers and organizations looking to implement embedding-based solutions. The cost efficiency is highlighted as one of the key benefits alongside accuracy and context length improvements.
questions.question: How much cheaper are Together Embeddings compared to other popular platforms?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI compatibility, which allows developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate. This means you can switch from OpenAI to Together by simply changing the base URL and API key. The endpoint is designed to make the migration process smooth for existing applications that already use OpenAI's embedding API.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility to make migrating easy.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint launched with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context. The M2-BERT models come in different context length variants including 2k, 8k, and 32k versions. Among these 8 models, some outperform both OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks.
questions.question: How many open source embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?
questions.explanation: The Together Embeddings endpoint was launched with exactly 8 open source embedding models, including UAE-Large-v1, BGE models, and M2-BERT retrieval models.

questions.lessonContent: To visualize sample data using the Together Embeddings endpoint, you first generate embeddings using the Together API by defining functions that call the API with your input texts. Once you have the embedding vectors, which for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K have a dimension of 768, you then transform these high-dimensional embeddings using t-SNE to reduce them to 2D for plotting. Finally, you plot the transformed embedding vectors to visualize how texts from different sources cluster together.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings data visualization process?

questions.lessonTitle: Configuring the Together Embeddings API Client
questions.lessonContent: To use the Together Embeddings endpoint with existing OpenAI-compatible code, you need to configure the client with a specific base_url. The Together Embeddings endpoint uses the base URL "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" which enables full OpenAI API compatibility. When initializing the OpenAI client, you provide your Together API key and set this base_url to redirect embedding requests to Together's servers. This configuration allows developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's more cost-effective embedding models without rewriting their entire codebase.
questions.question: What is the base_url required to use the Together Embeddings endpoint with OpenAI API compatibility?

questions.lessonContent: When making embedding requests to the Together API, you must specify the exact model string in your code. The API string format follows a specific pattern such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval" for the 8K context model or "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval" for the 32K long context model. The model parameter is passed directly to the client.embeddings.create() method when generating embeddings. This model specification determines both the embedding dimension and the maximum context length that will be used for processing your text.
